source_text: Ecce idem Moyses refert alio in loco, quod Abrahae uisus sit deus. quod nemo hominum deum uideat et utuat. potest deus, quomodo uisus est deus? quomodo uideri non potest? inquit, wdit umguam; hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. mentitur; ergo uere uisus est deus. ex quo intellegi potest, quod non pater uisus sit, qui numquam uisus est, sed filius, qui et descendere solitus est, et uideri quia descenderit. imago ro est enim éinuisibilis dei, ut mediocritas et fragilitas condicionis humanae deum patrem uidere aliquando iam tunc assuesceret in imagine dei, hoc est, in filio dei. gradatim enim et per incrementa fragilitas humana nutriri debuit per imaginem ad istam gloriam, ut deum patrem uidere possit aliquando, periculosa sunt enim quae magna sunt, si repentina sunt. nam etiam lux solis subita post tenebras splendore nimio insuetis oculis non ostendet diem, sed potius faciet caecitatem. quod ne in damnum humanorum contingat oculorum, paulatim disruptis et dissipatis tenebris, ortus luminaris istius mediocribus incrementis fallenter assurgens oculos hominum sensim assuefacit ad totum orbem suum ferendum per incrementa radiorum. sic ergo et Christus, id est imago dei et filius dei, ab hominibus inspicitur, qua poterat uideri. et ideo fragilitas et mediocritas sortis humanae per ipsum alitur, producitur, educatur, ut aliquando deum quoque ipsum patrem, assueta filium conspicere, possit, w est, uidere; ne maiestatis ipsius repentino et intolerabili fulgore percussa intercipi possit, ut deum patrem quem semper optauit uidere non possit. ex quo filius est hic qui uidetur; dei autem filius, dei uerbum est; dei autem uerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. quae, malum, ratio est ut dubitetur deus dici, qui tot modis deus intellegitur approbari? Ac si et Agar ancillam Sarae de domo eiectam pariter et fugatam angelus conuenit apud fontem aquae in uia Sur, fugae causas interrogat atque accipit, et post haec humilitatis consilia porrigit, spem praeterea illi materni nominis facit, quodque ex utero eius multum semen esset futurum spondet atque promittit, et quod Hismael ex illa nasci haberet, et cum ceteris aperit locum habitationis ipsius, actumque describit: hunc autem angelum et dominum scriptura proponit et deum (nam nec benedictionem seminis promisisset, nisi angelus et deus fuisset): quaerant quid in praesenti loco haeretici tractent. - pater fuit iste qui ab Agar uisus est, an non? quia deus positus sed absit deum patrem angelum dicere; ne alteri subsed angelum dicent fuisse. quomodo ergo deus erit, si angelus fuit, cum non sit hoc nomen angelis umquam concessum? nisi quoniam ex utroque latere nos ueritas in istam concludit sententiam, qua intellegere debeamus dei filium fuisse: qui, quoniam ex deo est, merito deus, quia dei filius, dictus sit, quoniam patri subditus et annuntiator paternae uoluntatis est, magni consilii angelus pronuntiatus est. ergo si hic locus neque personae patris congruit, ne angelus dictus sit, neque personae angeli, ne, deus pronuntiatus sit; personae autem Christi conuenit ut et deus sit, quia dei filius est, et angelus sit, quoniam paternae dispositionis annuntiator est: intellegere debent contra scripturas se agere haeretici, qui Christum cum dicant se et angelum credere, nolint illum etiam deum pronuntiare, quem in ueteri testamento ad uisitationem generis humani legunt\ saepe uenisse. Adhuc adiecit Moyses, Abrahae uisum deum apud quercum Mambre, sedente ipso ad ostium tabernaculi sui meridie, et nihilominus, cum tres conspexisset uiros, unum ex illis dominum nuncupasse; quorum cum pedes lauisset, cinericios panes cum butyro et ipsius copia lactis offert, et ut hospites retenti uescerentur, hortatur. post quae et quod pater futurus esset, audit; et quod Sara uxor eius paritura ex ipso filium esset, ediscit; et de exitu Sodomitarum, quae merebantur pati, recognoscit; et quod propter clamorem Sodomorum deus descendisset, addiscit. quo in loco si patrem uolunt uideri tunc fuisse cum angelis duobus hospitio receptum, patrem uisibilem haeretici crediderunt: si autem angelum, cum ex angelis tribus unus dominus nuncupatur, cur, quod non solet, angelus deus dicitur? nisi quoniam, ut deo patri inuisibilitas propria reddatur, et angelo propria mediocritas remittatur, non nisi dei filius, qui et deus est, Abrahae uisus et hospitio receptus esse credetur. quod enim erat futurus, meditabatur in sacramento Abrahae factus hospes, apud Abrahae filios futurus; cuius filiorum pedes, ad probationem quod ipse esset, abluit; reddens in filiis ius hospitalitatis, quod aliquando illi fenerauerat pater. unde et ne qua esset dubitatio quin iste Abrahae hospes fuisset, in Sodomitarum exitu ponitur: quoniam pluit dominus super Sodomam et Gomorram ignem et sulphur a domino de caelo. sic enim et prophetes ex persona dei: subuerti uos, inquit, sécut subuertit dominus Sodomam et Gomorram. dominus ergo Sodomam subuertit, id est, deus Sodomam subuertit: sed.in subuersione Sodomorum dominus pluit ignem a domino. hic autem dominus uisus est Abrahae deus: deus autem hic hospes est Abrahae uisus utique quia tactus. sed cum pater, quia inuisibilis, nec tunc utique uisus sit, uisus est et hospitio receptus et acceptus est, qui solitus est tangi et uideri: hic autem filius dei dominus a domino pluit super Sodomam et Gomorram sulphur atque ignem. hic autem dei uerbum est: uerbum autem dei caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. non pater igitur apud Abraham hospes, sed Christus fuit; nec tunc pater uisus est, sed filius; uisus autem est Christus. merito igitur Christus et dominus et deus est, qui non aliter Abrahae uisus est, nisi quia ante ipsum Abraham ex patre deo deus sermo generatus est. Adhuc, inquit, idem angelus et deus eandem Agar, fugatam de domo Abrahae cum puero, consolatur et uisitat. nam cum illa in solitudine exposuisset infantem, quia aqua defecisset ex utre, cumque puer ille clamasset, fletum et planctum leuasset, et audiuit, inquit scriptura, deus uocem pueri ae loco ubi erat. cum deum esse, qui uocem audisset infantis, rettulisset, adiecit: et uocauit angelus domini ipsam Agar de caelo; angelum referens esse quem deum dixerat, et~dominum pronuntians esse quem angelum collocarat.. quique angelus et deus adhuc ipsi Agar promittit maiora solacia, dicendo: ne timueris; exaudiui enim uocem pueri de loco ubi erat. surge, sume puerum, et tene: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum. hic angelus, si angelus tantum est, cur hoc sibi uindicat ut dicat: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum, cum hoc utique genus potentiae dei sit, angeli esse non possit? ex quo etiam deus confirmatur esse qui hoc potest facere. quoniam ut hoc ipsum comprobetur, adicitur per scripturam statim: e aperuit deus oculos eius, et uidit puteum aquae uiuae, et abiit, et impleuit utrem de puteo, et dedit puero, et erat deus cum puero. si ergo hic deus erat cum puero, qui aperuit oculos Agar, ut uideret puteum aquae uiuae et hauriret aquam propter urgentem sitis necessitatem; hic autem deus e caelo illam uocat; angelus dictus, cum superius uocem audiens clamantis pueri deus esset potius, non alius intellegitur quam angelus esse pariter et deus. quod cum patri competens et conueniens esse non possit, qui tantummodo deus est, competens autem esse possit Christo, qui non tantummodo deus sed et angelus pronuntiatus est, manifeste apparet non patrem ibi tunc locutum fuisse ad Agar, sed Christum potius, cum deus sit, cui etiam angeli competit nomen, quippe cum magni consili angelus factus sit; angelus autem sit, dum exponit sinum patris, sicut Ioannes edicit. si enim ipse Ioannes hunc eundem, qui sinum exponit patris, uerbum dicit carnem factum esse, ut sinum patris posset exponere, merito Christus non solum homo est, sed et angelus; nec angelus tantum, sed et deus per scripturas ostenditur, et a nobis hoc esse creditur, ne, si non Christum tunc locutum ad Agar uoluerimus accipere, aut angelum deum faciamus, aut deum patrem omnipotentem inter angelos computemus.
pass_a_gloss: Behold, Moses reports in another place that God was seen by Abraham. That no man of men sees God and uses. God can, how was God seen? How can he not be seen? He says, no man of men has ever seen; no one can see. He lies; therefore, God was truly seen. From which it can be understood that it was not the Father who was seen, who was never seen, but the Son, who was accustomed to descend and be seen because he had descended. For the image of the invisible God is the Son, so that the mediocrity and fragility of the human condition might become accustomed to see God the Father sometimes, even then, in the image of God, that is, in the Son of God. For human fragility ought to be nourished gradually and through increments to this glory, so that it might be able to see God the Father sometime, for great things are dangerous if they are sudden. For even the light of the sun, after darkness, does not show the day to unaccustomed eyes with too much splendor, but rather causes blindness. So that this might not happen to the detriment of human eyes, with the darkness gradually disrupted and dissipated, the rising of this luminary, slowly and gently ascending, accustoms human eyes to bear its whole orb through increments of rays. So also Christ, that is, the image of God and the Son of God, is seen by men, insofar as he can be seen. And therefore, the fragility and mediocrity of the human lot are nourished, produced, and educated through him, so that it might be able to see God the Father also, having become accustomed to see the Son; lest it be struck by the sudden and intolerable splendor of his majesty and not be able to see God the Father, whom it had always desired to see. From which it follows that the Son is the one who is seen; but the Son of God is the Word of God; and the Word of God was made flesh and dwelled in us; and this is Christ. What evil reasoning is it to doubt that he is called God, who is approved as God in so many ways? And if the angel met Hagar, the servant of Sarah, who was cast out and fled from her home, at the spring of water on the road to Sur, and inquired about the causes of her flight, and received them, and after these things, offered her counsel of humility, and gave her hope of the name of mother, and promised that there would be a great multitude from her womb, and that Ishmael would be born from her, and showed her the place of his habitation, and described his actions: let the heretics investigate what they treat in this present place. Was it the Father who was seen by Hagar, or not? Because God is posited, but it is absurd to call God the Father an angel; lest they say that another angel was present. How, therefore, can he be God if he was an angel, since this name is never conceded to angels? Unless, indeed, the truth from both sides concludes us to this sentence, that we ought to understand it was the Son of God: who, because he is from God, is rightly called God, because he is the Son of God, and because he is subject to the Father and the announcer of the Father's will, he is pronounced the angel of great counsel. Therefore, if this place neither suits the person of the Father, lest he be called an angel, nor the person of an angel, lest he be called God; but suits the person of Christ, that he is God, because he is the Son of God, and an angel, because he is the announcer of the paternal disposition: the heretics ought to understand that they act against the Scriptures, who, when they say they believe Christ is an angel, do not want to pronounce him God, whom they read in the Old Testament to have come often to visit the human race. Moreover, Moses added that God was seen by Abraham at the oak of Mamre, while he was sitting at the door of his tent at midday, and nonetheless, when he saw three men, he called one of them Lord; and when he washed their feet, he offered them ashes and bread with butter and an abundance of milk, and exhorted them to eat as retained guests. After these things, he heard that he would be a father; and that Sarah, his wife, would bear a son from him; and he recognized the exit of the Sodomites, who deserved to suffer; and he learned that God had descended because of the cry of Sodom. In this place, if they want the Father to have been seen then with two angels, received in hospitality, the heretics have believed in a visible Father: but if it was an angel, since one of the three angels is called Lord, why is an angel called God, which is not customary? Unless, indeed, that the invisibility proper to God the Father is restored, and the mediocrity proper to an angel is remitted, it is believed that it was not an angel, but the Son of God, who is also God, who was seen by Abraham and received in hospitality. For what was going to happen, he meditated in the sacrament, having become a guest of Abraham, among the sons of Abraham, to whom he would come; whose feet, as a proof that he was himself, he washed; rendering in the sons the right of hospitality, which the Father had once rendered to him. Whence also, lest there be any doubt that this guest of Abraham was he, it is placed in the exit of the Sodomites: because the Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord in heaven. For thus also the prophets speak in the person of God: I will overthrow you, he says, as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. Therefore, the Lord overthrew Sodom, that is, God overthrew Sodom: but in the overthrow of Sodom, the Lord rained fire from the Lord. But this Lord was seen by Abraham as God; and God is the guest seen by Abraham, certainly because he was touched. But when the Father, because he is invisible, was not seen then, he who is accustomed to be touched and seen was seen and received in hospitality: and this Lord, who rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah, is the Son of God; and the Word of God is the Word; and the Word of God was made flesh and dwelled in us; and this is Christ. Therefore, it was not the Father who was the guest with Abraham, but Christ; and it was not the Father who was seen then, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Therefore, Christ is rightly Lord and God, who was seen by Abraham in no other way than because, before him, Abraham was generated from God the Father as God the Word. Moreover, it is said that the same angel and God consoled and visited Hagar, who was cast out from Abraham's home with her child. For when she had exposed the infant in solitude, because the water had failed from the skin, and the child had cried out, and she had raised her weeping and lamentation, and the Scripture says that God heard the voice of the child from the place where he was; when it had been said that it was God who heard the voice of the infant, it was added: and the angel of the Lord called her, Hagar, from heaven; referring to the angel as the one whom he had called God, and pronouncing him Lord whom he had placed as an angel. And this angel and God promised greater solaces to Hagar, saying: Do not fear; for I have heard the voice of the child from the place where he was. Arise, take the child, and hold him; for I will make him a great nation. If this angel is only an angel, why does he claim this for himself, saying: for I will make him a great nation, since this is a kind of power proper to God, and it cannot be an angel's? From which it is also confirmed that he is God, who can do this. For in order to prove this very thing, it is added through Scripture immediately: and God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water, and she went and filled the skin from the well, and gave it to the child, and God was with the child. If, therefore, this was God with the child, who opened Hagar's eyes, so that she might see the well of living water and draw water because of the urgent necessity of thirst; and this God called her from heaven; and the angel is said to be the one who, hearing the voice of the crying child, was rather God, not another; it is understood that he is not only an angel, but also God. Which, since it is fitting and suitable for the Father, who is only God, cannot be; but it can be suitable for Christ, who is not only God, but also pronounced an angel; it clearly appears that it was not the Father who spoke then to Hagar, but rather Christ, since he is God, to whom the name of angel is also suitable, since he was made the angel of great counsel; and he is an angel, since he reveals the bosom of the Father, as John testifies. For if John himself says that this same one, who reveals the bosom of the Father, is the Word made flesh, so that he might reveal the bosom of the Father, it is right that Christ is not only man, but also angel; and not only angel, but also God, as the Scriptures show, and as we believe, lest, if we do not want to accept that Christ spoke then to Hagar, we either make an angel God, or compute God the Father among the angels.

pass_b_english: Moses records elsewhere that God appeared to Abraham, even though no human being has ever seen God. How, then, could God be seen if he cannot be seen? The text says no man has ever seen him, yet he was truly seen. From this we understand that the one seen was not the Father — who has never been seen — but the Son, who is accustomed to descend and make himself visible. The Son is the image of the invisible God, so that the frailty and limitations of our human condition might grow accustomed to seeing God the Father, even now, in the image of God — that is, in the Son of God. Human weakness had to be nurtured step by step toward that glory, so that one day it could bear the sight of the Father; sudden exposure to great things is dangerous. Just as the abrupt brilliance of the sun after darkness does not reveal the day to unaccustomed eyes but blinds them, God prevented such harm by letting the darkness fade gradually. The rising of this light ascended gently, accustoming human eyes to bear its full orb through increasing rays. In the same way, Christ — the image of God and the Son of God — is seen by human beings to the extent that he can be seen. Through him our frailty and lowliness are fed, developed, and trained, so that, having grown used to seeing the Son, we may someday see the Father also — lest the sudden, unbearable splendor of his majesty strike us down and keep us from seeing the Father we have always longed to see. Therefore the one seen is the Son; the Son of God is the Word of God; the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14); and this is Christ. What perverse reasoning would make us doubt that he is called God, when he is confirmed as God in so many ways? (Genesis 16:7-14)

Consider Hagar, Sarah's servant, cast out and fleeing. An angel met her at a spring on the road to Shur, asked the cause of her flight, listened, then gave her counsel of humility and the hope of motherhood, promising a vast offspring and that Ishmael would be born to her, even showing her where he would live. Scripture calls this visitor both angel and Lord and God — for he could not have promised such a blessing unless he were both angel and God. Let heretics examine what they make of this. Was it the Father whom Hagar saw? God is named, but it is absurd to call the Father an angel — unless they claim a different angel was present. How can he be God if he is an angel, since that title is never given to angels? Unless the truth from both sides drives us to this conclusion: the visitor was the Son of God. Because he is from God, he is rightly called God; because he is the Son, subject to the Father and the herald of the Father's will, he is named the Angel of Great Counsel (Isaiah 9:6). This passage fits neither the Father — lest he be called an angel — nor a mere angel — lest he be called God. It fits Christ, who is God as the Son of God, and angel as the announcer of the Father's purpose. Heretics who say they believe Christ is an angel yet refuse to call him God act against the Scriptures, which record his frequent visits to the human race in the Old Testament.

Moses adds that God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre while he sat at his tent door in the heat of the day (Genesis 18:1). When Abraham saw three men, he addressed one as Lord, washed their feet, and set before them bread, butter, and abundant milk, urging them to eat as honored guests. Then he heard that he would become a father, that Sarah would bear a son, learned the coming judgment on Sodom, and that God had descended because of its outcry. If heretics claim the Father was the one seen, hosted alongside two angels, they make the Father visible. But if it was an angel, why is one of the three called Lord and named God — which is not customary for angels? The only coherent reading: the invisibility proper to the Father is preserved, the humility proper to an angel is set aside, and the one seen and hosted is the Son of God, who is also God. He who was to come later among Abraham's descendants anticipated that future in a sacramental way, becoming Abraham's guest; he washed the feet of those descendants as proof of his identity, returning in the sons the right of hospitality the Father had once extended to him. To remove all doubt that this guest was the same person, the account continues with the destruction of Sodom: the Lord rained fire and sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord in heaven (Genesis 19:24). The prophets speak in God's person: 'I will overthrow you as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah' (Amos 4:11). So the Lord overthrew Sodom — that is, God overthrew Sodom — yet in that overthrow the Lord rained fire from the Lord. This Lord, seen by Abraham as God, is the guest Abraham touched. Since the invisible Father was not seen, the one accustomed to be touched and seen was seen and welcomed. This Lord who rained fire is the Son of God; the Word of God; the Word made flesh who dwelt among us (John 1:14); this is Christ. Therefore the guest with Abraham was not the Father but Christ; the one seen then was not the Father but the Son; Christ was seen. Christ is rightly Lord and God, seen by Abraham in no other way than that before him Abraham was begotten by God the Father as God the Word.

Again, the same angel and God consoled and visited Hagar, cast out with her boy (Genesis 16:7-14). When her water ran out and the child cried, she lifted up her weeping. Scripture says God heard the boy's voice where he lay. Having identified the hearer as God, the text then says the angel of the Lord called to Hagar from heaven — identifying the angel as the one just called God, and naming as Lord the one placed as angel. This angel and God promises greater comfort: 'Do not fear; I have heard the boy's voice. Rise, take the boy, hold him fast, for I will make him a great nation.' If he is only an angel, why does he claim the power to make a great nation — a power proper to God alone? This confirms he is God. To prove the point, Scripture immediately adds: God opened her eyes, she saw a well of living water, filled the skin, gave the boy drink, and God was with the boy. If this was God with the boy — who opened Hagar's eyes so she could see the well and draw water in her desperate thirst — and this God called from heaven, and the angel is said to be the one who, hearing the cry, was God, not another — then he is both angel and God. This cannot fit the Father, who is only God; but it fits Christ, who is not only God but also called angel. Clearly it was not the Father who spoke to Hagar, but Christ — God, to whom the name 'angel' also belongs, since he was made the Angel of Great Counsel, and angel because he reveals the Father's bosom, as John testifies (John 1:18). If John says this same one who reveals the Father's bosom is the Word made flesh, so that he could reveal that bosom, then Christ is rightly not only man but also angel; not only angel but also God, as Scripture shows and we believe — lest, refusing to accept that Christ spoke to Hagar, we either make an angel into God or count God the Father among the angels.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the visibility of the Son versus the invisibility of the Father, the dual nature of Christ as both God and Angel (Angel of Great Counsel), and the specific exegetical points regarding Hagar and Abraham. All scripture citations (Genesis 16, 18, 19; Isaiah 9:6; John 1:14, 18; Amos 4:11) are correctly identified and applied to the relevant clauses. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source.
